# Edelweiss

I consider myself far too sophisticated for musicals—too worldly, too critical, too aware of their manipulative swells of strings and improbable bursts into song. And yet there is one song that undoes me every time, that slips past every defense I've built: "Edelweiss." I cannot hear those opening notes without becoming, again, a little girl standing in my grandfather's living room, singing with all the earnest gravity a child can muster, while he sat in his worn armchair with a glass of scotch, laughing—not at me, but with a kind of tenderness that made the laughter itself feel like an embrace.

The lyrics themselves are deceptively simple: small and bright, clean and white, you look happy to meet me. As a child, I sang these words without understanding them, treating them as pleasant sounds strung together into a melody. But they carry a weight I didn't grasp until much later, a weight tied inextricably to my grandfather and the one true friendship of his life—a jeweler, a man who understood him in a way few others ever did, who shared his taste for scotch and his particular brand of quiet loyalty.

When the jeweler died, he left my grandfather something unexpected: a Rolex worth ten thousand dollars, an extravagant gift for a man who lived so modestly. My grandfather wore it constantly, every single day, though the metal turned his wrist an unmistakable green—a small, almost comic imperfection that he never once complained about. He wore it to dinner, to church, to ordinary Tuesday afternoons. And he wore it to the jeweler's funeral.

I remember that funeral vividly. The jeweler's daughter stood before the gathered mourners and sang "Edelweiss," her voice ethereal, otherworldly, rising and falling with a fragile beauty that seemed to hold the whole room in suspension. She could not tear her eyes from the casket as she sang, as though her gaze alone could keep her father tethered to this world a moment longer. And beside me, my grandfather wept openly, mouthing the words along with her, his fingers absently spinning the watch around his wrist—that green-stained, precious, irreplaceable gift—as if the motion itself were a kind of prayer.

The song ends with a plea: bless my homeland forever. It is a line about country, ostensibly, about patriotism and belonging. But sitting there, watching my grandfather grieve his only friend while wearing the last tangible piece of him, I understood the words differently. They became about loss, about memory, about the friendships that anchor us and the small, strange relics they leave behind. Every time I hear "Edelweiss" now, I am transported back to that living room, to that funeral, to the image of my grandfather's tears and his spinning watch—and I understand, finally, why a song about a flower can hold within it an entire lifetime of love.
outputs.L4:
**Edelweiss**

I was seven, maybe eight, standing on the ottoman
in my grandfather's den, the amber light of scotch
catching gold in his glass like something holy,
and he'd ask me to sing it again—
*Edelweiss, Edelweiss*—
that saccharine tune from a movie
about Nazis and nuns and a captain
who couldn't say the word *love*
except through flowers, except through song.

I didn't know yet what a song could hold.

My friend the jeweler once showed me his father's Rolex,
the one he inherited, the crystal scratched
from forty years of decades passing beneath it,
and he said *this is the only thing of his
that still keeps time*, and I thought
of my grandfather's hands, how they shook
near the end, how the scotch sat untouched,
how some things get passed down
not because they're valuable
but because someone held them once
and didn't know how else to say goodbye.

At the funeral, someone sang it.
Of course they did. The organ swelled
into that same simple melody,
small and white and blooming forever,
and I thought about how ridiculous it was—
a song from a musical, a song
that asks a flower to bless a homeland—
and yet the whole room was crying,
because grief doesn't care about sophistication,
grief will take whatever vessel is offered
and fill it to the brim.

I remember now: the last time,
it wasn't me singing to him.
He was ninety-one, his voice thin as paper,
and he sang it himself, alone,
scotch untouched, hands trembling
around the glass instead of the melody,
and halfway through he began to cry—
this man who taught me not to sob at war movies,
who called crying *the alarm system for cowards*—
he cried into *edelweiss, edelweiss*,
into every small and white thing,
into blessing his homeland forever,
and I understood then
that some songs are not about their words at all.

They are about the hands that hold the glass.
They are about the watch that still keeps time
though the man who wound it is gone.
They are about a man who spent his life
guarding his heart like a vault,
finally letting it snow open,
just once, singing to no one,
singing because some griefs
are too big for talking,
and only the simplest tune,
the one your granddaughter learned
before she understood loss,
could carry it.

# When the Cuckoo Calls

When spring arrives in the Alpine meadows, the landscape transforms into a symphony of sound and color. Among the most anticipated moments is when the first cuckoo calls echo through the valleys, signaling that winter has truly released its grip on the mountains.

The cuckoo, known for its distinctive two-note call, migrates back to European highlands each year, arriving just as the snow begins to retreat from the higher slopes. Local folklore has long associated the cuckoo's arrival with good fortune, and many mountain communities still celebrate the first call of the season as an unofficial start to spring.

Meanwhile, on the rocky outcrops and high meadows, edelweiss begins its slow emergence. This iconic Alpine flower, with its star-shaped white petals covered in fine, wool-like hairs, has become a symbol of the mountains themselves—representing purity, resilience, and the rugged beauty of high-altitude environments. Edelweiss typically blooms later than many other Alpine flowers, often not appearing until mid-summer, well after the cuckoo's early spring song has become a familiar backdrop to daily life in the mountains.

The relationship between these two natural phenomena—the cuckoo's call and the edelweiss bloom—creates a kind of seasonal calendar for those who live close to nature. When hikers hear the cuckoo, they know that weeks of warming weather lie ahead, eventually giving way to conditions perfect for edelweiss to flourish on its rocky perches.

Together, the sound of the cuckoo and the sight of edelweiss represent the changing seasons in Alpine regions—one announcing spring's arrival through song, the other confirming summer's presence through delicate, enduring beauty. Both have become woven into the cultural identity of mountain communities, celebrated in folk songs, stories, and traditions passed down through generations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that weaves song lyrics from "Edelweiss" (The Sound of Music) into a personal memory about a grandfather.
counterfactuals.output:
**What He Hummed in the Garden**

Grandpa's hands were soil and thread,
weathered maps of things he'd said
and things he'd never say out loud—
but every morning, clear and proud,
he'd hum some tune from a film he loved,
his slippers scuffing porch boards above
the roses he'd planted, row by row,
*small and white, clean and bright*,
the way he said edelweiss should grow.

I'd sit beside him, half-asleep,
while dew still clung to the marigolds' feet,
and he'd sing it soft, that old refrain—
*every morning you greet me*—
like the flowers themselves knew his name,
like the whole quiet yard was waiting
just to hear him sing again.

He never explained why he loved that song,
some film about a country gone wrong,
a family fleeing, a mountain's call,
but I think he saw himself in it all—
a man who'd bloomed in far off years,
carried oceans in his eyes, unseen tears,
and found this patch of earth to keep,
where the flowers he grew learned how to sleep
beneath his voice, low and slow:
*bloom and grow, bloom and grow forever.*

Now the porch is empty, the roses wild,
grown past the fence like an untamed child,
but some mornings, when the light comes thin
and gold across the grass, I let it in—
that hum, that half-remembered song,
and for a moment he's not gone,

just humming there among the green,
singing to the smallest, whitest thing,
his blessing folded soft and low—
*bless my homeland*, wherever that may be—
maybe just this yard, this memory,
this small forever he left for me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free verse poem using the italicized lyrics of "Edelweiss" as recurring refrains within a family narrative involving death and inheritance.
counterfactuals.output:
**Small and White**

*Edelweiss, edelweiss*—
that was the line he hummed
in the hospital bed, tuneless,
the oxygen mask fogging
each syllable into static.
We didn't know if he meant
the song or the flower
or the mountains he never climbed
except in the reel-to-reel films
stacked now in a box marked ESTATE.

*Every morning you greet me*—

and every morning after,
we woke to the same light
falling on the same brown carpet,
his voice gone from the kitchen,
his coffee cup still in the drainer
like an artifact from a dig site
no one wanted to catalogue.

The lawyer read the will
in a room that smelled of lemon polish.
My sister got the piano no one plays.
My brother got the truck, the tools,
the leather chair worn to the shape
of a man none of us
could ever quite sit into.

*Small and white, clean and bright*—

I got the edelweiss pin,
tarnished silver, pressed flat
in a velvet box that once held
something else, a ring maybe,
a name we never asked about.
He wore it on his lapel
every Sunday, said it was Austria,
said it was the war,
said it was a woman
whose face none of us have seen.

*You look happy to meet me*—

We are not happy.
We are counting spoons.
We are deciding who keeps
the photographs of people
none of us can name,
faces folding into strangers
the longer grief goes on.
This is what inheritance is:
not the house, not the money,
but the sudden weight
of every unanswered question
he took with him like luggage.

*Blossom of snow may you bloom and grow*—

The flower on the pin
doesn't grow anywhere near here.
It needs altitude, thin air,
rock to root in stubbornly.
Still, my daughter wears it now,
too young to know
what it means to bury a man
and inherit only the silence
where his stories used to be.

*Bloom and grow forever*—

Nothing does. Not the marriage
that ended before he did,
not the business he built
and let rust into rumor,
not even the grief itself,
which softens, which becomes
a habit of setting two coffee cups
before remembering.

*Edelweiss, edelweiss*—

We sang it at the funeral,
badly, off tune, the way
a family sings when it doesn't
know what else to do
with its hands, its throats,
the awful fact of a body
gone still under white cloth
like snow that fell overnight
and will not last the afternoon.

*Bless my homeland forever*—

His homeland was this kitchen,
this cracked linoleum,
this argument about the will
that is really an argument
about love, about who was loved more,
about the pin, the chair, the truck,
the small white flower
pressed flat and lying
in my daughter's palm
like a question
none of us
will ever finish asking.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary poem in the style of contemporary confessional poetry that mixes nostalgia, a grandfather's memory, a funeral, and quoted song lyrics.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Radio Remembers

The casket was too shiny for a man
who fixed his own truck in the gravel drive,
who smelled like WD-40 and spearmint gum,
who taught me that a whistle
could call a dog from a half-mile off
if you curled your tongue just right.

At the funeral home, someone had combed
his hair wrong—parted it on the side
he never wore it, and I wanted to reach in
and fix it, the way he'd reach across
the bench seat of his Ford
to fix my collar before church,
not saying a word, just *fixing*,
the way love moves through hands
when it can't move through mouths.

They played his favorite song at the reception—
some cousin's idea, or maybe his own,
written down somewhere in that shoebox
of instructions we found too late to argue with—
and the whole room went quiet
when the speaker crackled out
*"You are my sunshine, my only sunshine,"*
and I thought: liar,
you had six kids and thirteen grandkids
and a dog named Biscuit
and you loved us all like separate suns,
not one sunshine but a whole
solar system of stubborn light.

I keep the memory of him
in a coffee can now, like nails,
like something useful you save
for a repair you know is coming.
The whistle. The gum wrapper folded
into a perfect silver square.
The way he said *"hell"* like punctuation,
like a man who'd earned the right
to curse softly at broken things.

*"You'll never know, dear, how much I love you,"*
the song went on, and the room
cried the way rooms cry—
quietly, into styrofoam cups,
into the shoulders of people
we hadn't hugged in years.

I didn't cry until later,
alone in his workshop,
found a whistle he'd carved
from a chunk of cedar,
never finished, still rough
where his thumb would've smoothed it.

I put it to my lips.
No sound came out.
Just breath,
just air moving through a shape
he almost made complete.

*"Please don't take my sunshine away."*

I didn't sing it. I just thought it,
walking back into the kitchen
where his coffee cup still sat,
half-full, cold,
waiting for a mouth
that would never come back
to drink from it again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a prose poem that begins with "When I tell you I love the song 'Edelweiss'" and explores childhood memory, class anxiety about musicals, and grief.
counterfactuals.output:
When I tell you I love the song "Edelweiss," I mean I love it in the private way you love the plainest thing at a wedding—the water glass, the folded napkin—because it asks nothing of you. Not "Do-Re-Mi" with its ladder of ambition, not the twirl and gauze of "Sixteen Going on Seventeen," but this: a man alone with a guitar, singing to a flower that grows where almost nothing else can.

I grew up in a house where musicals were something other families did. We didn't have a piano. Didn't have a car that could get us to the city, or the forty dollars for two seats and a program you'd keep in a drawer forever, its pages gone soft from handling. My mother cleaned other people's houses. My father drove a truck for a company that eventually drove itself out of business. *The Sound of Music* came to us on a VHS tape recorded off television, commercials cut out badly, so the Captain's hand would freeze mid-gesture, then jump.

I watched it on the living room floor with the particular guilt of loving something soft. Boys where I grew up were supposed to want other things—engines, guns, girls with big hair, anything with an edge you could point at the world. I kept "Edelweiss" the way you keep a bruise you press just to feel it: alone, in the dark, rewinding.

My mother hummed it while she ironed. Not the words—she never learned the words—just the shape of it, that small ascending question at the end of each line, like something reaching for light through a crack in a floorboard.

She's been gone three years now and I still can't hear that song without my chest doing the thing it does, that clench, that fold, like a shirt she's pressing down to nothing. *Small and white, clean and bright*—edelweiss, meaning noble white, a flower that roots itself in rock faces where the air runs too thin for almost anything living, and still, something takes hold there. Something small. Something no one applauds for. Blooming anyway, blooming stubbornly, the way she is gone and I keep finding her regardless—in an ironing board left standing in an empty room, in a rerun at two in the morning, in the snow outside my window that keeps falling long after the credits should have ended, long after the house has gone dark, long after there is anyone left to turn it off.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short lyrical piece exploring how a beloved song connects generations, incorporating a specific anecdote about a jeweler's Rolex and a funeral scene.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Old Songs Carry

Grandpa wore his Rolex to the grave—
well, almost. Uncle stopped the casket lid,
slid it off his father's wrist that day,
said *this stays with the living*, and he did
what jewelers do: he polished up the past,
had it cleaned, the crystal buffed to shine,
gave it to my cousin, told him *this will last
longer than we do, longer than our time.*

At the funeral, someone played that song—
the one Grandpa hummed while fixing things,
the one that made the whole church sing along,
three generations finding what it brings:
my father's throat went tight, he knew each word,
my daughter, only six, began to sway,
she'd heard it first through headphones, undeterred
by decades—music doesn't fade away.

That's how it works, the way a melody
outlives the throat that first gave it a home.
The watch ticks on. The song won't let us be
forgotten in the ground, alone.
Some things we bury. Some we keep circling back—
a chorus, like a wrist that still knows time,
passed hand to hand along the family track,
still keeping perfect, unbroken rhyme.

We are the sum of songs we didn't write,
of jewels that outlast the ones who wear them,
of funerals that turn to something bright
when everybody rises up to share them—
one voice, then two, then all of us combined,
grandfather's hum becoming grandchild's shout,
the watch still ticking somewhere left behind,
the melody the only way we're found.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
